speaker: traver
text: Morning, everybody. Welcome to an oral argument session at the Fifth District Court of Appeal. My name is Dan Traver. I'm joined this morning on this panel by Judge Meredith Sasso and Judge Mary Nardello. I should advise you that this is being recorded. It's also being streamed live. This is case number 5D21-1841, Universal Property and Casualty Insurance Company versus Andre Modi as personal representative of the estate of Anirudh Modi. Mr. Lima, I believe you are the appellant in this case. I will assume, unless you tell me differently, that you'd like five minutes for rebuttal. Whenever you're ready, you may begin.

speaker: paulolima
text: Thank you, Your Honor. Good morning. May it please the court. My name is Paolo Lima here on behalf of the appellant, Universal Property Insurance. We start with, the reason we're here today is because the trial court erred in granting a directed verdict for the plaintiff in this trial as to liability. And it did so because it concluded, as a matter of law, that the insurance breaches of his post-loss policy conditions were not material. And so the main argument that we've made in our initial brief is that the evidence did not support a directed verdict here. Materiality of a breach is almost always an issue of fact. And if we look at the trial evidence as was set out in our brief, there was more than sufficient to, at the very least, create an issue of fact to submit those defenses to the jury. I don't believe that the plaintiff has even attempted to make a substantive defense of that decision on the merits. My reading of the answer brief is that they are relying on several different procedural arguments to support the judgment. So unless the court has any questions as to the main merits of the trial court's decision, I'll proceed to addressing the plaintiff's various arguments. The first one is invited error. The argument was that Universal's counsel invited the ruling made by the trial judge. We've cited some case law that we think is directly on point, specifically the S&I Investments case from the fourth DCA in 2010, which holds that it has to be for invited error to apply, the appellant has to have invited the specific ruling made by the trial court that they are now complaining of. And that just wasn't the case here. As we've sort of set out in detail in both our initial and the reply brief, the way it went down was that the defense counsel made the argument that the trial judge could decide as a matter of law that the breach was material if there had been no compliance at all. In other words, a breach with no attempts to comply with the policy conditions. And that was based on this case's, this court's holding in Starling from 2007. But counsel also noted that based on this court's Lopez decision, that if there is some compliance with a policy post-loss condition, well, that creates an issue of fact for the jury to decide. At no time did Universal's counsel argue that the court could decide as a matter of law that a breach was not material. And that is precisely the ruling that the trial judge made here.

speaker: paulolima

So even if there had arguably been a misstatement that the trial judge interpreted in a certain manner, there's no question that Universal's counsel then came around and gave the trial judge the opportunity to correct that error, which of course is the fundamental tenet of appellate review is was the trial judge given a chance to make the right ruling? And here he was, and the trial judge says, well, I'm sticking by my ruling. I've made my call and that's that. So for those reasons and everything else stated in the brief, we'd say the invited error doctrine just doesn't apply under the facts of these case. The next argument that they've raised is a pleading defect based on this court's ruling in Saavedra. And again, as we pointed out in detail in our reply brief, Saavedra certainly does say that you have to be specific in asserting affirmative defenses, but if you compare Universal's pleading in Saavedra versus Universal's pleading in this case, the pleading in this case, we would submit clearly passes muster under the Saavedra standard. In Saavedra, again, the Universal's response to the allegation that all conditions proceeding had been complied with was simply denied and strict proof thereof demanded. Here, on the other hand, the response to that allegation was Universal denies the allegations contained in paragraph 14, strict proof thereof is hereby demanded. Then it goes on to say, however, specifically, failure to provide prompt notice, failure to make reasonable and necessary repairs, failure to mitigate damages, failure to provide documents among other conditions. So there is a very specific denial there. Similarly, within the affirmative defense itself, in Saavedra, Universal merely stated that the plaintiff, quote, failed to satisfy all conditions proceeding to recover pursuant to the terms of the policy. Here, on the other hand, it, Universal pled that liability, if any, is only in accordance with the terms and provisions of the policy, but then it went on to reprint verbatim the relevant provisions of the policy. It identified the specific provisions that Universal relied on at summary judgment, and then again, at trial, specifically the prompt notice, the failure to protect the property, and the failure to provide records and documents that we request. So again, there has, it's a far cry from Saavedra. And in fact, in Saavedra, the court said, when sort of spelling out what the defendant had done wrong, this court wrote, at no point did Universal identify the nature of the conditions precedent or the nature of the noncompliance, such as the specific post loss duties with which Saavedra failed to comply, or where exactly in the policy such conditions could be found. As I've just read to the court, Universal did exactly in this case, what the court said in Saavedra needed to be done, needed to be fled. The next issue I'll sort of turn to is the plaintiff's contention in the answer brief that Universal denied coverage and therefore waived its right to demand compliance with the policy conditions, citing the fourth district's case in Bryant versus Giavera. That case is good law. However, it's certainly not applicable here because quite simply, Universal did not deny coverage. If you look at plaintiff's answer brief at page 26, in fact, they say Universal quote, confirmed coverage for the claim. And we'll look at, I'm looking at here, Universal's letter of February 7th, 2017. It's pages 1386 and 87 of the record. And it begins in the very second sentence of the letter. It says, although your claim damages are covered, are covered by your policy of insurance, repair costs must exceed the applicable policy deductible for claim payment to be considered. And so therefore we clearly do not have a denial of coverage and the Bryant case and that principle just doesn't apply here. There's been no waiver. Plaintiff raises another related issue, very, very similar that there's been an anticipatory breach by Universal. Again, it's based on this notion that Universal has denied coverage. As I've just read to you, there was no denial of coverage and therefore no anticipatory breach. The plaintiff relies on a fourth district's case in Goldberg, a case we're very familiar with that happened to be, you know, our firm had handled that appeal. And in Goldberg, the key language is the fourth district's pronouncement that an insurer quote, should not be deemed to have breached the contract where it accepted coverage and paid the only estimate it received of the actual cash value of the loss. Now here, Universal did accept coverage of Dr. Modi's claim. It did not make a payment, but again, the only reason for that is, is because the only estimate of damages fell below the policy deductible. And at no time prior to filing suit, did plaintiff ever provide a competing estimate saying, well, yes, I understand Universal's position that the damages fall below the policy deductible, but here's my estimate for more money and that's what you need to pay me. Never happened in this case. And under Goldberg, the holding is, unless you submit a competing estimate, there's no anticipatory breach. And so we would say that that does not apply either. The final argument that they've raised in the answer brief, and again, we've addressed in our reply brief, certainly rely on our reply, is that Universal needed to request compliance with these policy conditions and it didn't request compliance and therefore somehow perhaps it's been waived. We point out, first of all, that two of the three policy conditions relied upon by Universal don't request any additional or don't require any additional requests for compliance. One is to give prompt notice. The other is to protect the property from further damage. Both of those conditions are self-executing by the very language of the policy. In other words, you can't expect Universal to request a plaintiff to give prompt notice of a claim other than in the policy. Until you tell me there's a claim, I can't request you to give prompt notice other than what we've already done, which is by putting into the policy, you have a claim, you have to give prompt notice. The only other, and so that alone would be sufficient to support a reversal, but just to tie it all up, the third condition does require a request because it says that the plaintiff is required to provide us with records and documents we request. And as we've stated in our brief, Universal made multiple requests for additional documents to support the claim. Most notably, the most direct one came on March 15th, 2017 in a letter and email. There's different language in the cover email as well as the letter that was actually sent to plaintiff's public adjuster. And the email says, please forward your estimate of damages, walk through photographs and any additional information you believe will be helpful for us in the evaluation of this claim. The testimony is that it's unrebutted that at no time prior to filing suit did the plaintiff provide any of those documents. In fact, the only two documents that were ever submitted prior to suit were the notice of claim and a letter requesting appraisal under the policy. Last thing I'll note is that there's some argument in the answer brief that some of these communications went to an administrative assistant at plaintiff's public adjuster, a woman by the name of Nora Catano. And that, I guess the argument is that she wasn't authorized to act on plaintiff's behalf. But if you look at the trial evidence, again, that is clearly not the case. Plaintiff's public adjuster is a man named Kevin Downs and he was asked at trial whether his assistant, Ms. Catano, routinely communicated with the insurance companies on behalf of their clients. And he said, yes, it happened all the time. And if you look at this case itself, Ms. Catano is the only one who actually ever communicated with Universal. She's the one who reported, who sent the email reporting the claim to Universal. She's the one who sent the letter, emailed the letter requesting appraisal. And plaintiff's own testimony during his deposition, he passed away prior to trial, but his deposition testimony, which was played at trial to the jury was quote, Nora Catano, she's the administrator of Five Star Claims Adjusting. She sent a letter explaining everything to Universal. So plaintiff's own understanding is clear that Ms. Catano was authorized to speak on his behalf. And so for that reason, we would say that that last argument raised by the plaintiff in the answer brief does not apply and doesn't warrant a reversal. Unless the court has any further questions, I'll reserve the remainder of my time for rebuttal.
